This decision including any ﬁnding of facts, impairment and sancƟ on is an appealable
decision under The General PharmaceuƟ cal Council (Fitness to PracƟ se and DisqualiﬁcaƟ on

2
etc. Rules) Order of Council 2010. Therefore, this decision will not take eﬀect unƟ l 29 July
2026 or, if an appeal is lodged, once that appeal has been concluded. However, the interim
suspension set out in the decision takes eﬀect immediately and will lapse when the decision
takes eﬀect or once any appeal is concluded.

3
ParƟ culars of AllegaƟ on
You, a registered pharmacist,
1. Were convicted at Inverness Sheriﬀ Court and JusƟ ce of the Peace Court on 31
July 2025 of three oﬀences in contravenƟ on of the Sexual Oﬀences (Scotland)
Act 2009, SecƟ on 6.
As a result of the maƩ ers set out above, your ﬁtness to pracƟ se is impaired by reason of
convicƟ on
DocumentaƟ on

Document 4 – Bundle of correspondence with the Registrant
DeterminaƟ on
IntroducƟ on
1.
This is the wriƩ en determinaƟ on of the Fitness to PracƟ se CommiƩ ee at the General
PharmaceuƟ cal Council (‘the Council’).
2.
This is the Principal Hearing of Mr Goncalo De Melo Rodrigues, a registered
pharmacist under registraƟ on number 2081610 (‘the Registrant’).
3.
This hearing is governed by The Pharmacy Order 2010 (‘the Order’) and The General
PharmaceuƟ cal Council (Fitness to PracƟ se and DisqualiﬁcaƟ on etc. Rules) Order of
Council 2010 (‘the Rules’).
4.
The statutory overarching objecƟ ves for these regulatory proceedings (‘the
ObjecƟ ves’) are:

To protect, promote and maintain the health, safety and well-being of the public;

To promote and maintain public conﬁdence in the professions regulated by the
Council; and

To promote and maintain proper professional standards and conduct for
members of those professions.

4
5.
The CommiƩ ee also has regard to the guidance contained in the Council’s Good
decision making: Fitness to pracƟ se hearings and outcomes guidance as revised
March 2024 (‘The Guidance’).
6.
A Principal Hearing has up to three stages:
Stage 1. Findings of Fact – the CommiƩ ee determines any disputed facts.
Stage 2. Findings of ground(s) of impairment – the CommiƩ ee determines
whether, on the facts as proved, a statutory ground for impairment is established
and, if so, whether the Registrant’s ﬁtness to pracƟ se is currently impaired.
Stage 3. SancƟ on – the CommiƩ ee considers what, if any, sancƟ on should be
applied if the Registrant’s ﬁtness to pracƟ se is found to be impaired.
Service of NoƟ ce of Hearing
7.
The CommiƩ ee has seen a leƩ er dated 21 May 2026 from the Council headed ‘NoƟ ce
of Hearing’ addressed to the Registrant and sent to his registered email address
noted on the Register. The CommiƩ ee noted that this was more than the 28 days
required by Rule 16. The CommiƩ ee saw the entry on the register where the
Registrant had been marked as saying yes to receiving important communicaƟ ons via
email and noted that he had replied to emailed correspondence. The CommiƩ ee
considered that the Registrant had agreed to receiving correspondence via email.
8.
The CommiƩ ee was therefore saƟ sﬁed that there had been good service of the
NoƟ ce of Hearing (‘NoƟ ce’) in accordance with Rules 3 and 16 of the Rules.
ApplicaƟ on to proceed in the absence of the Registrant
9.
The Registrant was not in aƩ endance at this hearing, nor was someone aƩ ending on
their behalf. The CommiƩ ee heard submissions from Mr Hamlet, on behalf of the
Council to proceed in the absence of the Registrant under Rule 25. He submiƩ ed that
the Registrant had given a clear indicaƟ on by email that he had no intenƟ on of
aƩ ending. It was appropriate and fair to proceed in the absence of the Registrant.
The allegaƟ ons are suﬃciently important for there to be an imperaƟ ve to proceed
given that there is no reason to adjourn. Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that the Registrant
had an obligaƟ on to update the GPhC as to their contact details and could not “put
their head in the sand” so as to derail the proceedings.
10.
The CommiƩ ee noted the following record of communicaƟ on with the Registrant.

5

22 January 2026 email from GPhC to the Registrant requesƟ ng response to
enable service

26 January 2026 – follow up email from GPhC to the Registrant

27 January 2026 – Documents sent to the Registrant by special delivery

02 February 2026 09:52 email from GPhC to the Registrant to say access to
online documents would be emailed.

02 February 2026 12:08 – noƟ ﬁcaƟ on that the Registrant had accepted the
invitaƟ on to the shared online document folder

02 February 2026 12:11 email from Registrant in response to earlier email from
GPhC

06 February 2026 email from GPhC to the Registrant detailing available support
services

08 June 2026 email from GPhC to the Registrant serving the Council’s bundle

16 June 2026 email from GPhC to the Registrant asking if there was anything he
would wish to provide to the CommiƩ ee
11.
There had been one email from the Registrant in response to an email about service
of documents on 02 February 2026 which said “I don't live in the UK. I've not been
able to work since 2024, how do you expect me to pay or aƩ end anything? Please
don't bother me any longer, I've dealt with a well over-exaggerated penalty for
something I'm not to blame for. This is pure harassment and excuses to hide
racism……., my family has suﬀered enough, I have no money in my account, please
stop. …………. STOP”
12.
The CommiƩ ee accepted the advice of the Legally Qualiﬁed Chair.
13.
The CommiƩ ee decided to proceed in the absence of the Registrant for the following
reasons:

The CommiƩ ee consider that the Registrant has responded to an email dated
02 February 2026 that would mean he is aware of the existence of the Fitness
to PracƟ se proceedings. The CommiƩ ee has found good service of the NoƟ ce,
therefore the Registrant is, or should be, aware of the hearing today.

The Registrant has not responded to mulƟ ple further emails from the Council
despite being aware of the proceedings. The CommiƩ ee ﬁnds that the one
response from the Registrant clearly indicates that he does not wish to
engage with the Council. The NoƟ ce of Hearing indicates that this hearing is
taking place remotely so the Registrant could have aƩ ended even if he is not

6
in the UK. The CommiƩ ee have therefore considered that the Registrant has
chosen to voluntarily absent himself from this hearing.

The Registrant did not indicate that any other date would be more suitable
for the hearing and did not request that the hearing be adjourned. The
CommiƩ ee ﬁnds that there is no informaƟ on to suggest an adjournment
would result in the Registrant’s aƩ endance in future.

There is a public interest in the expediƟ ous disposal of cases especially as
these allegaƟ ons are of a serious nature.
Background
14.
The Registrant is a registered Pharmacist who was, at the relevant Ɵ me, working as a
locum at Boots Pharmacy in West Scotland.
15.
The case concerns the Registrant’s convicƟ on on three counts of “intenƟ onally
causing another to look at a sexual image without consent” under SecƟ on 6 of the
Sexual Oﬀences (Scotland) Act 2009. The oﬀences concerned three female colleagues
and occurred between May 2023 and October 2025.
16.
Witness 1 in an interview with a Manager at Boots, on 10 August 2023, states that
she was approached by Colleague A. The account provides that Colleague A showed
Witness 1 a video sent to her by the Registrant of a “woman having an orgasm”.
Witness 1 states that Colleague A was visibly upset and said she did not want to work
with him as a result.
17.
Colleague B gave an interview to a Store Manager on 10 August 2023. She describes
meeƟ ng the Registrant through Facebook and thereaŌ er he began to send her
pictures of himself that became increasingly inappropriate, culminaƟ ng in him
sending her photos of his penis. She states that she was very upset.
18.
Colleague C has provided a detailed wriƩ en account, undated. She states that the
Registrant messaged her and complimented her, despite her making it clear that she
was married. The messages became increasingly personal, culminaƟ ng in him
‘sexƟ ng’ her and making sexually explicit comments. These included a comment that
“He’d like to bend me over the desk at work and that work was a “kink” of his”. She
describes being sent a disappearing message by the Registrant and being encouraged
to open it. Upon opening it, she found it was a picture of his erect penis. She
described feeling sick and violated.
19.
Concerns in respect of the Registrant’s conduct were originally raised with the
Council by a Superintendent Pharmacist at Boots in October 2023 , who relayed
reports from female members of staﬀ in the West Scotland area that the Registrant
had sent them unsolicited videos and images via social media. It is reported that the

7
local area manager aƩ empted to make contact with the Registrant to discuss the
concerns and the response was to deny any wrongdoing.
20.
The Registrant was arrested by Police Scotland on 11 November 2023 and convicted
on 31 July 2025. He received a concurrent Community Payback Order, supervised
over 6 months.
Decision on Facts
21.
The allegaƟ on in this case is a convicƟ on. The CommiƩ ee had sight of the full extract
convicƟ on report of the three oﬀences and therefore found the convicƟ ons and facts
proved in accordance with Rule 24(4).
22.
Having found the parƟ culars of allegaƟ on proved, the CommiƩ ee went on to
consider whether the Registrant’s ﬁtness to pracƟ se is currently impaired by reason
of their convicƟ on.
Decision on Impairment
Council’s Submissions
23.
Mr Hamlet directed the CommiƩ ee to the Guidance. Mr Hamlet’s oral submissions
can be summarised as follows:
24.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that the oﬀences took place within a professional context. The
nature of the oﬀending amounted to the targeƟ ng of female colleagues and
persistent pursuit of them even when they had been clear that they were not
interested. Mr Hamlet suggested there was a clear risk to members of the public
from a repeat of this type of behaviour. He submiƩ ed that the fact that the Registrant
has targeted colleagues and having formed an appropriate relaƟ onship has then
persistently imposed unwanted inappropriate behaviour showed a modus operandi
that illustrates a risk to the public. Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that the Registrant’s email
on 02 February 2026 showed that the Registrant was in denial of his wrongdoing, he
considered that he was not to blame which showed that he had a conƟ nued lack of
insight. Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that this increased the risk to the public.
25.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that this type of oﬀending brings the profession into disrepute.
He further submiƩ ed that the oﬀending has breached the fundamental principles of
pharmacy namely treaƟ ng colleagues with respect. He suggested that the Registrant
has persistently targeted young female colleagues.
26.
Mr Hamlet said that although there is very liƩ le conduct that is totally beyond
remediaƟ on, this behaviour shows a parƟ cular aƫ
tude. He said that the Registrant
has not provided evidence that he understands the nature of the wrongdoing or the
impact of the behaviour on his colleagues and the public. He pointed out that the
Registrant has not engaged with the proceedings except to deny his wrongdoing, he
aƩ acks the punishment he received. He submiƩ ed that the Registrant claimed that

8
he was being harassed and subjected to racism which Mr Hamlet suggested meant
he was puƫ
ng himself as the vicƟ m. Mr Hamlet further suggests that this email
shows that the Registrant has no insight, which heightens the risk of repeƟ Ɵ on. Mr
Hamlet suggested that the Registrant has not reﬂected or repented.
27.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that a ﬁnding of current impairment is necessary to restore
and uphold the standard of the profession and also to maintain public conﬁdence. He
submiƩ ed that the CommiƩ ee could ﬁnd impairment on each of the three
ObjecƟ ves.
Registrant’s posiƟ on
28.
The Registrant was not present and had not submiƩ ed any wriƩ en submissions for
the hearing. The CommiƩ ee noted from the email of 02 February 2026 that the
Registrant appears to conƟ nue to deny any blame and the CommiƩ ee considered
that the Registrant did not accept that he was impaired.
Decision
29.
The CommiƩ ee accepted the advice of the Legally Qualiﬁed Chair.
30.
The CommiƩ ee took account of the guidance given to the meaning of ‘ﬁtness to
pracƟ se’ in the Council’s publicaƟ on “Good decision-making” (Revised March 2017).
Paragraph 2.11 reads:
“A pharmacy professional is ‘ﬁt to pracƟ se’ when they have the skills,
knowledge, character, behaviour and health needed to work as a
pharmacist…safely and eﬀecƟ vely. In pracƟ cal terms, this means maintaining
appropriate standards of competence, demonstraƟ ng good character, and
also adhering to the principles of good pracƟ ce set out in our various
standards, guidance and advice.”
31.
In considering whether the Registrant’s ﬁtness to pracƟ se is currently impaired the
CommiƩ ee considered whether the parƟ culars found proved show that acƟ ons of
the Registrant:
• present an actual or potenƟ al risk to paƟ ents or to the public;
• has brought, or might bring, the profession of pharmacy into disrepute;
• has breached one of the fundamental principles of the profession of
pharmacy;
32.
The CommiƩ ee also considered whether:
• the conduct which led to the complaint is able to be addressed
• the conduct which led to the complaint has been addressed

9
• the conduct which led to the complaint is likely to be repeated
• a ﬁnding of impairment is needed to declare and uphold proper standards of
behaviour and/or maintain public conﬁdence in the profession.
33.
The CommiƩ ee considered that the Registrant’s oﬀences caused harm to all three
colleagues. Colleague C describes feeling anxious, angry, violated, traumaƟ sed and
physically sick. She has subsequently experienced recurring sexual assault dreams as
a result of the Registrant’s behaviour. The other two colleagues were said to be upset
with Colleague A being observed to be distressed. The CommiƩ ee considers that this
behaviour would have created a risk of harm to the public because harm was caused
to colleagues and working relaƟ onships would be impacted. Colleague A said that
she did not want to work with the Registrant at all. The CommiƩ ee considered that
Colleagues had been made to feel uncomfortable in their place of work. The
CommiƩ ee considered that this can cause a lack of focus on paƟ ents that could
thereby cause them harm. The CommiƩ ee considers that sexual misconduct of this
nature, intenƟ onally imposing sexual images on colleagues without their consent,
clearly breaches professional boundaries and the relaƟ onship of trust between
colleagues. In one case the vicƟ m was aged only 19 and therefore the Registrant
would have been in a posiƟ on of relaƟ ve power over her as a result. The behaviour
was repeated and was persistent in the face of a clear lack of consent and was
repeated with mulƟ ple colleagues over a signiﬁcant Ɵ me period. The behaviour was
repeated despite concerns being raised with the Registrant by an area manager in
2023. The CommiƩ ee considered that these elements of the behaviour mean that
there is a risk of repeƟ Ɵ on with an accompanying risk of harm to the public and to
colleagues.
34.
The CommiƩ ee considers that the oﬀences have breached the fundamental
principles of the pharmacy profession treaƟ ng people with dignity and respect. The
Registrant repeatedly pursued this conduct despite a clear lack of consent. The
CommiƩ ee considers that behaviour of this nature brings the profession of pharmacy
into disrepute. The Registrant has 3 convicƟ ons for sexual oﬀences against diﬀerent
vicƟ ms who were his pharmacy colleagues resulƟ ng in a community sentence. The
Registrant has repeatedly breached the trust put in him by colleagues and the public
to act professionally and maintain professional boundaries. This type of behaviour
undermines trust in the profession as vulnerable paƟ ents need to be able to rely on
professionals that care for them not breach the boundaries of the posiƟ on of trust
they are placed in.
35.
The CommiƩ ee considered that the Registrant’s behaviour breached Standard 6 of
the GPhC” Standards for Pharmacy Professionals May 2017 - ‘Pharmacy professionals
must behave in a professional manner, are trustworthy and act with honesty and
integrity.’ That standard speciﬁes “ People expect pharmacy professionals to behave
professionally. This is essenƟ al to maintaining trust and conﬁdence in pharmacy.

10
Behaving professionally is not limited to the working day, or face-to-face interacƟ ons.
The privilege of being a pharmacist or pharmacy technician, and the importance of
maintaining conﬁdence in the professions, call for appropriate behaviour at all
Ɵ mes.” The CommiƩ ee consider that the oﬀences of this nature are the anƟ thesis of
the professional behaviour expected and the registrant has behaved in a way that
will undermined trust and conﬁdence in the pharmacy profession.
36.
The CommiƩ ee considers that sexual oﬀending of this nature is diﬃcult to remediate.
The CommiƩ ee has no informaƟ on about the compleƟ on of the Registrant’s criminal
sentence. The Registrant has not engaged with the Fitness to PracƟ se proceedings.
The CommiƩ ee has had no evidence of remorse, remediaƟ on, insight or anything
that would address the concerns outlined above. The only communicaƟ on has been
a statement from the Registrant four months aŌ er his criminal sentence was imposed
that he was not to blame, which the CommiƩ ee ﬁnds does not evidence insight. The
CommiƩ ee ﬁnds that the Registrant has not remediated or addressed his oﬀending
behaviour. The CommiƩ ee therefore considers that there remains a real risk of
repeƟ Ɵ on of the behaviour which has an accompanying risk of harm to the public
and colleagues. The CommiƩ ee considers that a ﬁnding of impairment is necessary
to protect the public.
37.
The CommiƩ ee further ﬁnds that a repeƟ Ɵ on of such behaviour would bring the
profession into disrepute and breach the fundamental principles of pharmacy. The
CommiƩ ee considers that the serious nature of this criminal conduct, that has not
been in any way remediated would mean that a ﬁnding of impairment is necessary in
the wider public interest to mark the seriousness of what has occurred and
therefore to uphold and maintain professional standards and public conﬁdence in the
profession.
38.
The CommiƩ ee therefore ﬁnds the Registrant’s current ﬁtness to pracƟ se to
be impaired on public protecƟ on and public interest grounds.
Decision on SancƟ on
39.
Having found impairment, the CommiƩ ee has gone on to consider the maƩ er of
sancƟ on. The CommiƩ ee’s powers are set out in ArƟ cle 54(2) of the Order. The
CommiƩ ee should consider the available sancƟ ons in ascending order from least
restricƟ ve, take no acƟ on, to most restricƟ ve, removal from the Register, in order to
idenƟ fy the appropriate and proporƟ onate sancƟ on that meets the circumstances of
the case.
40.
The purpose of the sancƟ on is not to be puniƟ ve, though a sancƟ on may in fact have
a puniƟ ve eﬀect. The purpose of the sancƟ on is to meet the overarching objecƟ ves
of regulaƟ on, namely the protecƟ on of the public, the maintenance of public

11
conﬁdence and to promote professional standards. The CommiƩ ee is therefore
enƟ tled to give greater weight to the public interest over the Registrant’s interests.
41.
The CommiƩ ee had regard to the Council’s Good decision making: Fitness to pracƟ se
hearings and outcomes guidance as revised March 2024 (‘The Guidance’) to inform
its decision.
Council’s Submissions
42.
The CommiƩ ee took into account the submissions made by Mr Hamlet which can be
summarised as follows:
43.
Mr Hamlet conﬁrmed to the CommiƩ ee that the reference on the extract of
convicƟ on to “Sexual Oﬀences Act 2003” cerƟ ﬁcaƟ on was a reference to the fact that
the nature of the convicƟ ons and sentence meant that the Registrant was subject to
noƟ ﬁcaƟ on requirements and would therefore be on the Sex Oﬀenders Register for a
period of 5 years from the date of his convicƟ on.
44.
Mr Hamlet referred the CommiƩ ee to the following secƟ ons of the Guidance:

5.2 - Key factors to consider

5.3 – ProporƟ onality

5.7 – Public interest

5.10 – MiƟ gaƟ ng/AggravaƟ ng factors

5.13-5.14 Circumstances

5.17 – Behaviour and Aƫ
tude

5.19 – Insight and remediaƟ on

6.2-6.7 Sexual Misconduct
45.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that this case had the following aggravaƟ ng factors:

the gravity of the conduct underlying the convicƟ ons

the mulƟ ple vicƟ ms involved

the status of the vicƟ ms as work colleagues

the period over which the conduct occurred

the absence of evidence of any acknowledgement of wrongdoing, insight or
remorse

the absence of evidence of any aƩ empt at remediaƟ on

the risk of repeƟ Ɵ on
46.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed there were no miƟ gaƟ ng factors in the case. Mr Hamlet went
on to address the outcomes as outlined in secƟ on 4.3 of the Guidance. He submiƩ ed
that taking no acƟ on and giving a warning were not suitable outcomes given the
seriousness of the oﬀences and the risk to the public that had been idenƟ ﬁed. Mr

12
Hamlet submiƩ ed that condiƟ ons were not appropriate as they would fail to reﬂect
the gravity of the oﬀending and the imposiƟ on of condiƟ ons would not send an
appropriate message to the public or to the profession. He further submiƩ ed that
there were pracƟ cal consideraƟ ons relaƟ ng to what condiƟ ons would be workable
given the risk to the public idenƟ ﬁed.
47.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that suspension may protect the public and might meet the
gravity of the wrongdoing. However, as a suspension is only for up to 12 months, to
consider a suspension the CommiƩ ee would need to see evidence of remorse and be
able to envisage a pathway back to unrestricted pracƟ ce. In the absence of those
things a suspension order would be bound to fail if no lesser risk would be posed at
its conclusion.
48.
Mr Hamlet submiƩ ed that removal was the only appropriate outcome in this case
because the seriousness of the behaviour meant that it was fundamentally
incompaƟ ble with being a registered professional.
Registrant’s posiƟ on
49.
The Registrant had not provided the CommiƩ ee with any evidence or submissions.
The CommiƩ ee noted that his posiƟ on was that he was not to blame.
Decision
50.
The CommiƩ ee accepted the advice of the Legally Qualiﬁed Chair.
51.
The CommiƩ ee ﬁrst considered what, if any, aggravaƟ ng and miƟ gaƟ ng factors there
may be. The CommiƩ ee idenƟ ﬁed the following aggravaƟ ng factors:

Three convicƟ ons which involved three diﬀerent vicƟ ms

Harm was caused to vicƟ ms

Persistent breach of the trust between colleagues

One vicƟ m aged 19

Conduct repeated over 2 years, despite the Registrant being spoken to by an
area manager about his behaviour in 2023

The absence of any evidence of remorse, insight or remediaƟ on
52.
The CommiƩ ee did not idenƟ fy any miƟ gaƟ ng factors on the informaƟ on before it.
53.
The CommiƩ ee went on to consider the available outcomes in ascending order
starƟ ng with the least restricƟ ve. The CommiƩ ee must idenƟ fy the least restricƟ ve
and proporƟ onate outcome that in the parƟ cular circumstances adequately

13
addresses the overarching objecƟ ves of regulaƟ on;  the protecƟ on of the public, the
maintenance of public conﬁdence and the need to promote professional standards.
54.
To take no acƟ on: The Guidance indicates that “This may apply even when
impairment is found, but there is no risk to the public or need to decide on a diﬀerent
outcome.” The CommiƩ ee considered that this outcome would not be appropriate
given the seriousness of the maƩ er and the fact that the CommiƩ ee has idenƟ ﬁed a
risk to the public.
55.
Advice: The Guidance indicates that “Advice can only be given to a professional when
no impairment is found.” The CommiƩ ee therefore found that this outcome was not
available in this case as impairment was found.
56.
Warning:  The Guidance indicates that this outcome may apply when: “There is a
need to demonstrate to a professional, and more widely to the profession and the
public, that the conduct or behaviour fell below acceptable standards. There is no
need to take acƟ on to restrict a professional’s right to pracƟ se, there is no conƟ nuing
risk to paƟ ents or the public, but there needs to be a public acknowledgement that
the conduct was unacceptable.” The CommiƩ ee ﬁnds that this outcome would not
reﬂect the seriousness of the behaviour given that there are criminal convicƟ ons for
sexual oﬀences and the conƟ nuing risk idenƟ ﬁed by the CommiƩ ee.
57.
CondiƟ ons of RegistraƟ on: The Guidance indicates that this outcome may be
appropriate where: “ There is evidence of poor performance, or signiﬁcant
shortcomings in a professional’s pracƟ ce, but the commiƩ ee is saƟ sﬁed that the
professional may respond posiƟ vely to retraining and supervision. There is not a
signiﬁcant risk posed to the public, and it is safe for the professional to return to
pracƟ ce but with restricƟ ons.”
The CommiƩ ee considers that this outcome is not appropriate. There is a signiﬁcant
risk posed to the public and the nature of the risk involving overstepping boundaries
is not one that can be addressed by condiƟ ons and the nature of the behaviour itself

In relaƟ on to removing a pharmacist from the register, the Guidance states:

The CommiƩ ee has also considered the following paragraphs of the Guidance

“Sexual misconduct – whatever the circumstances – undermines public trust in the

In some circumstances it can present a signiﬁcant and immediate risk to paƟ ent

15
assault, physical examinaƟ ons of paƟ ents that are without consent or unnecessary,

The misconduct can take place in many seƫ
ngs. This can be:

ng with family members

63.
The CommiƩ ee considers that the serious nature of the repeated oﬀending and the

The CommiƩ ee considered that there are three convicƟ ons for sexual oﬀences that

16
this oﬀending cannot be reconciled with those principles. The CommiƩ ee considers

The Committee considers removal from the register to be the only necessary and
